Below is a **complete but exam-friendly guide to Agile** , covering Agile vs Waterfall, Agile values/principles, major frameworks, Scrum roles/events/artifacts, a simulated sprint, Kanban, XP, Lean, and when to use each. **1. What is Agile?** **Agile** is an approach to software/project development where work is done in **small, incremental cycles** , with continuous customer feedback and frequent delivery of working products. Instead of trying to define everything at the beginning, Agile allows requirements to **evolve as the project progresses** . **Simple example** Suppose a company wants to build an **online banking application** . Instead of developing everything for 12 months and delivering at the end: - Sprint 1 → Login - Sprint 2 → Account balance - Sprint 3 → Fund transfer - Sprint 4 → Bill payment - Sprint 5 → Notifications Customers provide feedback after each increment. **2.

Agile vs Waterfall** | **Aspect** | **Waterfall** | **Agile** | |----------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------| | Approach | Sequential | Iterative & incremental | | Requirements | Defined early | Can evolve | | Delivery | Usually at the end | Frequent/incremental | | Customer involvement | Mainly beginning/end | Continuous | | Change | Difficult/costly | Expected and welcomed | | Testing | Often after development | Continuous | | Planning | Detailed upfront | Adaptive | | Feedback | Late | Frequent | | Risk | Discovered later | Identified early | | Best for | Stable requirements | Changing requirements | | Team structure | Often functional | Cross-functional | | Example | Construction of a bridge | Mobile application | **Waterfall** Requirements ↓ Design ↓ Development ↓ Testing ↓ Deployment ↓ Maintenance **Agile** Plan → Develop → Test → Review ↑ ↓ └──── Feedback ──────┘ Sprint 1 Plan → Develop → Test → Review Sprint 2 ... **Example** If a government project has **fixed legal requirements** , Waterfall may work well. If you're developing a **new mobile app** where customers may continuously request changes, Agile is generally more suitable. **3. Agile Manifesto – 4 Values** The Agile Manifesto has **4 core values** . **1. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools** People and communication are more important than blindly following tools/processes. **Example:** A developer and tester discuss a defect directly rather than exchanging 20 emails. **2.

Working software over comprehensive documentation** Documentation is useful, but delivering something that actually works is more valuable. **Example:** Instead of spending 3 months creating specifications, deliver a working login feature early. It does NOT mean "no documentation." **3. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation** Work closely with the customer rather than relying only on the original contract. **Example:** Customer says: "Users actually need OTP login instead of password-only login." Agile team discusses and adapts. **4. Responding to change over following a plan** A plan is important, but responding to useful change is more important than blindly following it. **Example:** A competitor launches a new feature. The team can reprioritize the backlog. **4. Agile Principles – 12 Principles** **1. Early and continuous delivery** Deliver valuable software early and frequently. **2. Welcome changing requirements** Even late changes can be accepted when they provide value. **3. Frequent delivery** Deliver working software frequently. **4. Business and developers work together** Business stakeholders and technical teams collaborate continuously. **5. Build motivated teams** Give teams the environment and support they need. **6. Face-to-face communication** Direct communication is highly effective. **7. Working software is the primary measure of progress** Progress is demonstrated through working product increments. **8. Scrum Framework** **Scrum** is one of the most widely used Agile frameworks. Scrum works through fixed-length iterations called **Sprints** . Typical Sprint: **1–4 weeks** Commonly: **2 weeks** Product Backlog ↓ Sprint Planning ↓ Sprint Backlog ↓ Sprint ↓ Daily Scrum ↓ Increment ↓ Sprint Review ↓ Sprint Retrospective ↓ Improvement **7. Scrum Roles** Modern Scrum terminology calls these **accountabilities** . There are **3 primary Scrum accountabilities** : 1. Product Owner 2. Scrum Master 3. Developers **7.1 Product Owner** The Product Owner is responsible for **maximizing product value** and managing the Product Backlog.

Developers **7.1 Product Owner** The Product Owner is responsible for **maximizing product value** and managing the Product Backlog. **Responsibilities** - Define product vision - Understand customer needs - Create/refine backlog items - Prioritize backlog - Define/review acceptance criteria - Communicate with stakeholders - Accept/reject completed work based on agreed criteria **Example** For an online banking application: Product Owner prioritizes: 1. Login 2. Account balance 3. Fund transfer 4. Bill payment 5. Investment Why? Because login and account access provide more immediate value. **7.2 Scrum Master** The Scrum Master is responsible for helping everyone understand and use Scrum effectively and for improving the team's effectiveness. **Responsibilities** - Facilitate Scrum events - Remove/resolve impediments - Coach team - Protect Scrum principles - Help improve collaboration - Help organization understand Scrum **Example** Developer says: "I cannot test the payment API because another team's service is unavailable." Scrum Master helps remove the impediment by coordinating with the other team. **Important** **Scrum Master is NOT the traditional project manager.** They don't simply assign tasks to developers. **7.3 Developers** Developers are the people who create the usable product Increment. They may include: - Software developers - Testers - Automation engineers - UX specialists - Database engineers - DevOps engineers **Responsibilities** - Design - Coding - Testing - Integration - Documentation where necessary - Code review - Delivering a usable Increment The team collectively decides **how** to accomplish the Sprint Goal. **8.

Scrum Events / Ceremonies** The five formal Scrum events are: 1. Sprint 2. Sprint Planning 3. Daily Scrum 4. Sprint Review 5. Sprint Retrospective **Backlog refinement/grooming** is important Scrum work, but it is **not a formal Scrum event** in the current Scrum Guide. **9. Sprint** A Sprint is a fixed-length period during which the team creates a usable Increment. Usually: **2 weeks** Example: Monday Week 1 → Friday Week 2 10 working days During the Sprint: - Development happens - Testing happens - Daily Scrum happens - Backlog is refined - Product Increment is created **10. Sprint Planning** Sprint Planning answers three major questions: **1. Why?** What is the **Sprint Goal** ? **2. What?** Which Product Backlog Items will be worked on? **3. How?** How will the Developers accomplish the work? **Example** Sprint Goal: "Allow customers to securely log into the banking application." Selected stories: US1 – Login with username/password US2 – Password validation US3 – Account lock after 5 failures US4 – Logout The team then decomposes them into tasks. **11. Daily Scrum** A short daily event, normally **15 minutes** , for Developers. Purpose: Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. Example: **Developer A:** Completed login API. Today I'll integrate authentication. **Developer B:** Completed UI. Today I'll integrate API. **Tester:** Started login testing. Blocked by missing test data. **Scrum Master:** Will help resolve the test-data issue. **Important** Daily Scrum is **not a status meeting for the manager** . **12.

**Tester:** Started login testing. Blocked by missing test data. **Scrum Master:** Will help resolve the test-data issue. **Important** Daily Scrum is **not a status meeting for the manager** . **12. Sprint Review** Held at the end of the Sprint. The team demonstrates the Increment to stakeholders and gathers feedback. Example: Team → Demonstrates Login ↓ Customer feedback ↓ "Add biometric login" ↓ Product Backlog updated The Review is about **product inspection and feedback** , not merely presenting slides. **13. Sprint Retrospective** The team discusses: **What went well?** **What didn't go well?** **What should we improve?** Example: | **Area** | **Discussion** | |-------------|-------------------------------| | Good | Automation tests increased | | Problem | Test environment was unstable | | Improvement | Create environment monitoring | | Owner | DevOps | | Target | Next Sprint | The goal is **continuous improvement** . **14. Backlog Refinement / Grooming** Backlog refinement means continuously preparing upcoming Product Backlog Items. Activities include: - Clarifying requirements - Breaking large stories - Adding acceptance criteria - Estimating - Removing obsolete items - Reordering/prioritizing Example: Large requirement: "Build payment system." Break into: Payment ├── Add beneficiary ├── Enter amount ├── Validate balance ├── OTP verification ├── Process payment └── Generate receipt **15. Product Backlog** An ordered list of everything that may be needed in the product. Example: Product Backlog 1. Login 2. Account balance 3. Fund transfer 4. Bill payment 5. Notifications 6. Investment The Product Owner orders it based on value, risk, dependencies, etc. **17. Sprint Backlog** Contains: - Sprint Goal - Selected Product Backlog Items - Plan for delivering them Example: Sprint Goal: Enable secure customer login Sprint Backlog: ✓ Login UI ✓ Login API ✓ Password validation ✓ Account lock ✓ Logout **18. Increment** The usable result produced during the Sprint. Example: At the end of Sprint 1: Working login functionality integrated into the application. The Increment should satisfy the **Definition of Done** . **19. Definition of Done** The Definition of Done describes the quality standard that must be satisfied before work is considered complete. Example: A story is Done when: - Code completed - Code reviewed - Unit tests passed - Integration tests passed - No critical defects - Security checks passed - Documentation updated where required - Deployed to agreed environment **20. User Story** Agile commonly expresses requirements as user stories. **Format** **As a [user], I want [function], so that [benefit].** Example: As a banking customer, I want to log in using my username and password so that I can securely access my account. **Acceptance Criteria** Given valid credentials When user clicks Login Then user should reach dashboard **21. Kanban** Kanban is an Agile method focused primarily on **visualizing work and optimizing flow** . Typical Kanban board: BACKLOG TODO IN PROGRESS TEST DONE Login Search Payment Login Profile Checkout Cart API Search Logout **Key concepts** - Visualize work - Limit Work in Progress (WIP) - Manage flow - Make policies explicit - Improve continuously **24. WIP Limit** WIP = **Work In Progress** Suppose: IN PROGRESS WIP Limit = 2 Only 2 items can be actively worked on. If two developers finish their tasks, they pull new work. This prevents: 10 tasks started 0 tasks completed Instead: Start → Finish → Start → Finish **25. Kanban Example** Software support team receives unpredictable production issues. Board: New → Analysis → Development → Testing → Done If production issues arrive continuously, fixed two-week Sprints may not be ideal. Kanban allows the team to continuously pull the highest-priority work. **26. Major practices include: - Pair programming - Test-driven development (TDD) - Continuous integration - Refactoring - Simple design - Small releases - Collective code ownership - Customer involvement **Example of Pair Programming** Two developers work together: Developer A → writes code Developer B → reviews/thinks Then they switch. Benefits: - Better code quality - Knowledge sharing - Early defect detection **27. TDD** TDD = **Test-Driven Development** Cycle: RED ↓ Write failing test ↓ GREEN ↓ Write minimum code to pass ↓ REFACTOR ↓ Improve code Example: Requirement: Password must contain at least 8 characters. First write the test. Input: abc Expected: Invalid Then implement the code. **28. Lean** Lean focuses on **maximizing customer value while eliminating waste** . Typical wastes include: 1. Waiting 2. Defects 3. Overproduction 4. Unnecessary processing 5. Unnecessary movement 6. Inventory 7. Transportation 8. Underutilized people/talent **Example** A developer waits 3 days for a test environment. That's **waiting waste** . Lean asks: How can we reduce or eliminate this waiting? **29.

When Should You Use Which?** **Use Scrum when:** - Product development is iterative - Requirements change - You can work in Sprints - A dedicated Product Owner exists - Team can create increments regularly **Example:** Developing a new healthcare application. **Use Kanban when:** - Work arrives continuously - Priorities change frequently - Support/maintenance is important - You need continuous delivery **Example:** Production support team. **Use XP when:** - Software quality is critical - Requirements change frequently - Technical complexity is high - Strong engineering discipline is needed **Example:** Mission-critical software requiring extensive automated testing and frequent releases.

Pros and Cons** **Scrum** **Advantages** - Clear structure - Frequent delivery - Regular feedback - Transparency - Continuous improvement - Good team collaboration **Disadvantages** - Too many meetings if poorly implemented - Requires disciplined team - Can struggle with constantly changing urgent work - Poor Product Owner involvement can hurt the project **Kanban** **Advantages** - Simple and visual - Flexible priorities - Continuous delivery - Excellent for support teams - WIP limits improve focus **Disadvantages** - Less structure than Scrum - Easy to misuse as simply a task board - Long-term planning can be harder - Requires good workflow discipline **XP** **Advantages** - Excellent software quality - Early defect detection - Strong engineering practices - Continuous integration - Excellent knowledge sharing **Disadvantages** - Pair programming can be expensive - Requires technically mature developers - Practices can be difficult to adopt - Less suitable when team culture doesn't support close collaboration **Lean** **Advantages** - Reduces waste - Improves efficiency - Focuses on customer value - Encourages continuous improvement - Can reduce cost and cycle time **Disadvantages** - Can be difficult to identify all forms of waste - Overemphasis on efficiency can be harmful - Requires organizational culture change - Benefits may take time to appear **32.

Quick Decision Guide** What kind of work? | ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Product with Continuous Quality/ Sprints incoming engineering | work | ↓ ↓ ↓ SCRUM KANBAN XP | | Need to improve efficiency/waste? | ↓ LEAN **In real organizations, you don't necessarily choose only one.** For example: **Software product team:** **Scrum + XP + Lean practices** Could mean: - Scrum → Sprint management - XP → TDD, CI, pair programming - Lean → eliminate waste - Kanban → visualize workflow/WIP So Agile methods can be **combined** . **33. One Complete IT Example** Suppose you're developing a **Healthcare Claims Processing System** . **Product Owner** Defines: "Claims should be processed faster and with fewer errors." **Product Backlog** 1. Claim submission 2. Claim validation 3. Duplicate detection 4. Eligibility verification 5. Claim processing 6. Payment calculation 7. Reporting **Scrum** Team works in 2-week Sprints. **Sprint Planning** Selects: Claim submission Claim validation Duplicate detection **Daily Scrum** Team discusses progress and impediments. **Development** Developers use: - TDD - Code reviews - Continuous integration - Automation testing **Sprint Review** Demonstrate working claim submission and validation. **Retrospective** Team identifies: "Testing started too late." Improvement: QA participates during story development. **Kanban** Team uses a board: To Do → Development → Code Review → Testing → Done **Lean** Team discovers: Developers wait 2 days for test data.
